title: How Ripperology Works
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant examine whether Jack the Ripper could have been the British impressionist painter Walter Sickert. They cover the 1888 Whitechapel (Canonical) murders, the amateur field of ripperology, and suspects police have named over the years. They discuss crime novelist Patricia Cornwell's 2002 claim that Sickert was the Ripper, based on her reading of his paintings such as "The Camden Town Murder" (alternate title "What Shall We Do for Rent?") and on mitochondrial DNA matching from Ripper letters. They note the flaws in both arguments: art is open to interpretation, mitochondrial DNA traces only maternal lineage and matched around fifty men in London, and a ripperologist said Sickert wrote only some fraudulent letters. The episode ends with the sign-off and a pointer to the HowStuffWorks article.

segments.title: Opening and introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode and the question of whether Jack the Ripper could have been an artist.

segments.title: Walter Sickert and the Ripper murders
segments.summary: Walter Sickert, a British impressionist painter aged 28 during the 1888 Whitechapel murders, is proposed as a suspect. The hosts describe the victims as alcoholic, middle-aged prostitutes and note that the killer was never caught and that ripperology grew up as amateur investigation, with about 170 suspects named by police.

segments.title: Patricia Cornwell's art-based theory
segments.summary: Crime novelist Patricia Cornwell named Sickert in 2002. She read some of his paintings as confessional, possibly depicting murdered prostitutes as models, and noted his training under James Whistler, who advised painting from life. The hosts note a 1990s FBI profile suggesting the killer may have vented rage through art or fantasy writing.

segments.title: Camden Town Murder painting and DNA evidence
segments.summary: Cornwell's key painting, The Camden Town Murder, was read as a confession, though it has an alternate title, What Shall We Do for Rent. She also bought paintings, tore one apart, and drew criticism from the Royal Academy's curator. Her hard evidence was mitochondrial DNA, which traces only maternal lineage and matched about fifty people in London, one of them Sickert, using DNA from Ripper letters.

segments.title: Ripper letters and conclusion
segments.summary: Cornwell found that Sickert wrote one or two of the hundreds of letters ostensibly from the Ripper, but a ripperologist argued this only shows he wrote fraudulent letters, not that he was the killer.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to the HowStuffWorks article and invite feedback by email.
